div.p: Microsoft Windows Firewall Observability collects, parses, normalises and visualises two complementary data sources from your Windows workstations and servers:

tr.td: Every connection allowed or dropped by Windows Defender Firewall

Windows Event Log
Windows Firewall With Advanced Security / Firewall
Every change to firewall settings, rules and service state

div.p: Knowledge objects are compliant with the Splunk Common Information Model: Network Traffic for the connection log and Change for the configuration events.

ol.li: Install this app on your search heads. The dashboards and detections live there.
Install Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (8.9.0 or later) on the same tier. It provides the Windows Event Log field extractions this app builds on.
Open Configuration in the app navigation bar and declare the index that receives the firewall data. This writes the windows_firewall_index macro.
Deploy the default/inputs.conf stanzas of this app to every Windows forwarder, adapting the index value to your indexing policy. Restart or reload the forwarder afterwards.
Enable firewall logging on the Windows hosts (next section).

div.div: Upgrading from 2.x? The setup page of version 2.x wrote a macro named windows_pfirewall_index while every search used windows_firewall_index, so the configured index was silently ignored. This is fixed in 3.0.0 — re-run the setup page once after upgrading.

ol.li: Press Windows + R, type wf.msc and press Enter.
Right-click Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security on Local Computer and choose Properties.
For each profile tab (Domain, Private, Public), click Customize under Logging.
Set Log dropped packets and Log successful connections to Yes.
Raise Size limit to at least 20480 KB so the file does not rotate every few minutes.

div.p: Or through PowerShell, on all three profiles at once:

Or through Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security > Windows Defender Firewall Properties > (profile) > Logging > Customize.
div.div: The Splunk forwarder service account must be able to read C:\Windows\System32\LogFiles\Firewall\. Running the forwarder as Local System is the simplest way to guarantee that.
div.p: Two macros carry the base filter. Prefer them over hard-coded index and sourcetype clauses.

div.h1: Going further — the three optional data sources
div.p: The app works with the two mandatory sources above. Three optional additions each unlock a specific view. None of them is required, and none of them changes anything if left off.

tr.td:
WFP audit events
Security 5157 and 5152, optionally 5156
Process Attribution view and the Processes panel of Host 360 and Peer Pivot: which binary opened the connection.
5157 and 5152 are moderate. 5156 is very verbose — it logs every permitted connection. Start without it.

TA-windows-firewall-posture
on the forwarders
Firewall Posture view: which hosts are unprotected right now, and which ones cannot log at all.
~144 small events per host per day, plus one rule inventory per day.
Makes the Overview instant on large estates.
Indexer CPU and summary disk. Start with a 7 day summary range.

div.p: Audit policy on the monitored hosts:

pre.code:
# Blocked connections and dropped packets - moderate volume auditpol /set /subcategory:"Filtering Platform Connection" /failure:enable auditpol /set /subcategory:"Filtering Platform Packet Drop" /failure:enable
# Allowed connections (event 5156) - VERY verbose, enable deliberately # auditpol /set /subcategory:"Filtering Platform Connection" /success:enable

div.p: Then point the wfo_wfp_index macro at the index holding your Security events — from the Configuration page, or directly in Settings > Advanced search > Search macros. The app reads whatever sourcetype you already use (XmlWinEventLog:Security or WinEventLog:Security) and normalises everything at search time, so there is nothing to re-ingest and no conflict with Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows.
div.div: On a domain controller, event 5156 can reach tens of thousands of events per minute. Enable the success audit on a single test host first and measure before rolling out.

ol.li: Settings > Data models > Windows Firewall Observability > Edit > Edit acceleration, tick Accelerate, pick a summary range (7 days is a good start).
Wait for the model to build — the same page shows the progress.
Return to the app Configuration page and set Data model accelerated to yes. This flips the wfo_summariesonly macro.

div.div: Until step 3, the Overview still works — it just searches raw data. If you set it to yes before acceleration has built, the Overview will show nothing.

div.p: The app ships 24 saved searches. All alerts are disabled by default — review the thresholds against your own baseline, then enable them from Settings > Searches, reports and alerts. Highest value first:

ul.li: Firewall Disabled On Host and Default Inbound Action Set To Allow — the two changes that silently remove all protection.
Administrative Protocol Exposed — RDP, SMB, SSH, WinRM or a database port answering a public address.
Possible C2 Beaconing — outbound sessions at a near constant interval.
Port Scan and Network Sweep Detected — reconnaissance visible in the denied traffic.
Host Stopped Sending Firewall Logs — collection health, so an empty dashboard never gets mistaken for a quiet network.

div.p: lookups/whitelist_ip_ranges.csv drives the `ip_whitelist` macro and the Noise filter input present on every dashboard. Add your own trusted ranges to it:
Matching is done in CIDR on both src_ip and dest_ip: an event is dropped as soon as either end belongs to a listed range.

tr.td: Dashboards are empty
Run the Windows Firewall - Data Collection Health report. If it returns nothing, the index declared in the setup page does not match the one used by your forwarders.
Traffic stops after a while, then resumes
The log file rotated. Version 3.0.0 sets initCrcLength = 2048 in inputs.conf precisely to survive that — make sure your forwarders received the new file.
Fields are shifted by one column
Older Windows builds log 17 columns, newer ones 18. Version 3.0.0 uses a regex extraction that handles both. Confirm you are not overriding REPORT-Network_Traffic locally.
No configuration change events
Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows is required for the Event Log field extractions, and the WinEventLog input must use renderXml = 1.
Timestamps are off
Windows writes the firewall log in local time. Set TZ on the host props or on the forwarder if it differs from the indexer.
